notes:
1. Agriculture — Importance and Economic Role

  • Agriculture is a foundational part of the Indian economy and belongs to the primary sector.
  • It provides food, employment, rural income, livelihood security and raw materials for several industries.
  • Its importance extends well beyond its direct contribution to national output.
📌 Must-Memorise

Agriculture → Primary Sector

2. Agriculture — Linkages with Industry

Agriculture supplies raw materials to industries such as:

  • Textiles → Cotton and fibres.
  • Sugar → Sugarcane.
  • Food processing → Farm produce.
  • Edible oils → Oilseeds.
  • Dairy processing → Milk.
  • Leather → Livestock-related inputs.

3. Farm Income — Wider Rural Economy

Higher agricultural income can increase rural demand for:

  • Housing.
  • Transport.
  • Education.
  • Consumer goods.
  • Machinery.
  • Services.

4. Agricultural Exports

Important agricultural and allied exports include:

  • Rice.
  • Spices.
  • Tea.
  • Coffee.
  • Marine products.
  • Cotton.
  • Processed foods.

5. Declining Output Share — Continuing Importance

  • Agriculture's relative share in national output has declined over time.
  • However, it remains critical for food security, rural livelihoods, employment and industrial linkages.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Lower GDP Share ≠ Agriculture Is Unimportant

6. Structural Features of Indian Agriculture

Indian agriculture is characterised by:

  • Diverse climate and soils.
  • Regional variation in rainfall and irrigation.
  • Small and marginal holdings.
  • Significant monsoon dependence.
  • Coexistence of subsistence and commercial farming.
  • Seasonal and disguised unemployment in some regions.

7. Small and Marginal Holdings

Small holdings can create difficulties in:

  • Mechanisation.
  • Bargaining power.
  • Credit access.
  • Storage.
  • Risk absorption.

However, small farms can still achieve high productivity when supported by irrigation, technology, credit, extension and markets.

8. Monsoon Dependence and Irrigation

  • A significant part of Indian agriculture remains dependent on monsoon rainfall.
  • Irrigated farming is generally more stable than purely rain-fed agriculture.
  • Productivity therefore varies significantly across regions depending on water availability and infrastructure.

9. Subsistence and Commercial Farming

Subsistence farming:

  • Primarily serves household consumption and livelihood needs.

Commercial farming:

  • Is oriented more strongly towards market sale and profit.
  • Both forms coexist in India.

10. Seasonal and Disguised Unemployment

  • Seasonal unemployment arises because agricultural labour demand varies across cropping seasons.
  • Disguised unemployment arises when more workers are engaged than are actually needed.

11. Cropping Seasons — Kharif, Rabi and Zaid

India's three main cropping seasons are:

  • Kharif.
  • Rabi.
  • Zaid.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kharif → Monsoon

Rabi → Winter

Zaid → Summer

12. Kharif Season

  • Kharif crops are generally sown with the onset of the southwest monsoon.
  • They are harvested after the monsoon season.
  • Their performance is strongly influenced by monsoon rainfall.

Important Kharif crops include:

  • Rice.
  • Maize.
  • Cotton.
  • Groundnut.
  • Soybean.
  • Millets.
  • Several pulses.

13. Rabi Season

  • Rabi crops are generally sown during cooler months after the monsoon.
  • They are harvested in spring or early summer.
  • Irrigation becomes especially important where winter rainfall is limited.

Important Rabi crops include:

  • Wheat.
  • Barley.
  • Gram.
  • Mustard.
  • Certain pulses.

14. Zaid Season

  • Zaid is the short summer cropping season between Rabi and Kharif.

Common crops include:

  • Watermelon.
  • Cucumber.
  • Vegetables.
  • Fodder.
  • Other short-duration crops.

15. Rice — Major Food Crop

  • Rice is one of India's most important food crops.
  • It generally requires warm conditions and adequate water.
  • It is widely grown in irrigated or high-rainfall regions.
  • It is especially important in southern, eastern and northeastern India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rice → Important Kharif Crop

16. Tamil Nadu — Rice

  • Tamil Nadu is an important rice-producing State.
  • Paddy cultivation is particularly significant in the Cauvery Delta.

17. Wheat — Major Rabi Crop

  • Wheat is one of India's major food grains.
  • It is primarily a Rabi crop.
  • It generally requires cool conditions during growth and warmer conditions during ripening.
  • Production is concentrated mainly in northern and central India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Wheat → Rabi

18. Millets — Dryland Crops

Important millets include:

  • Jowar.
  • Bajra.
  • Ragi.
  • Many millets require less water than paddy.
  • They are suited to dry and semi-arid regions.
  • They are also nutritionally important.
📌 Must-Memorise

Millets → Dryland + Lower Water Requirement

19. Pulses — Protein and Soil Fertility

Important pulses include:

  • Gram.
  • Tur.
  • Urad.
  • Moong.
  • Lentils.
  • Pulses are important sources of plant protein.
  • Many pulse crops improve soil fertility through biological nitrogen fixation.

20. Rhizobium and Pulses

  • Rhizobium bacteria are closely associated with nitrogen fixation in pulse crops.
📌 Must-Memorise

Pulses → Rhizobium → Nitrogen Fixation

21. Maize — Multiple Uses

Maize is used for:

  • Human consumption.
  • Animal feed.
  • Starch.
  • Other industrial purposes.

22. Commercial Crops — Meaning

  • Commercial crops are grown mainly for sale, processing or industrial use.

Important examples include:

  • Cotton.
  • Sugarcane.
  • Oilseeds.
  • Jute.
  • Plantation crops.

23. Cotton

  • Cotton is an important fibre crop.
  • It supplies raw material to the textile industry.
  • It grows well under warm conditions.
  • Cotton is associated with black soils in several regions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cotton → Fibre + Black Soil Association

24. Sugarcane

  • Sugarcane is an important commercial crop.
  • It is used for sugar, jaggery and ethanol.
  • It has a relatively long growing period and requires substantial water.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sugarcane → Sugar + Jaggery + Ethanol

25. Oilseeds

Major oilseeds include:

  • Groundnut.
  • Mustard.
  • Soybean.
  • Sunflower.
  • Sesame.
  • They provide raw material to the edible-oil industry.

26. Jute

  • Jute is an important natural fibre crop.
  • It requires warm and humid conditions.
  • Its cultivation has historically been concentrated in eastern India.

27. Plantation Crops

Important plantation crops include:

  • Tea.
  • Coffee.
  • Rubber.

28. Tea — Major Producing Regions

Important tea-producing regions include:

  • Assam.
  • West Bengal.
  • Tamil Nadu.
  • Kerala.
  • Tea requires suitable rainfall, temperature and well-drained soils.

29. Coffee — Southern Concentration

  • Coffee cultivation is concentrated mainly in southern India.
  • Karnataka is the leading coffee-producing region according to the supplied material.
  • Kerala and Tamil Nadu also contribute.
📌 Must-Memorise

Coffee → Karnataka Leading Region

30. Natural Rubber

  • Natural rubber requires warm and humid climatic conditions.
  • It is cultivated mainly in suitable southern and northeastern regions.

31. Irrigation — Meaning and Importance

  • Irrigation means artificial supply of water to crops.
  • It reduces dependence on uncertain rainfall.
  • Reliable irrigation supports multiple cropping and more stable agricultural production.
📌 Must-Memorise

Irrigation → Artificial Supply of Water

32. Major Sources of Irrigation

Important sources include:

  • Canals.
  • Wells.
  • Tube wells.
  • Tanks.
  • Reservoirs.

33. Canal Irrigation

  • Canal irrigation carries water from rivers, reservoirs or dams to agricultural fields.
  • It is important in several river-basin regions.

34. Wells and Tube Wells

  • Wells and tube wells provide groundwater irrigation.
  • They offer flexible access to water but excessive extraction can deplete aquifers.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Groundwater Irrigation → Useful but Can Be Unsustainable

35. Tank Irrigation

  • Tanks store monsoon water for local agricultural use.
  • Tank irrigation has historically been important in peninsular India.

36. Tamil Nadu — Tank-Irrigation Tradition

  • Tamil Nadu has a long tradition of tanks and interconnected irrigation systems.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu → Strong Tank-Irrigation Tradition

37. Micro-Irrigation

  • Micro-irrigation supplies controlled quantities of water to crops.
  • It improves water-use efficiency.

The two major methods are:

  • Drip irrigation.
  • Sprinkler irrigation.

38. Drip Irrigation

  • Drip irrigation supplies water directly near plant roots.
  • It reduces evaporation and runoff losses.
  • It is particularly useful in water-scarce regions and for many high-value crops.
📌 Must-Memorise

Drip → Water Near Roots

39. Sprinkler Irrigation

  • Sprinkler irrigation distributes water over fields in a pattern similar to rainfall.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sprinkler → Artificial Rainfall Pattern

40. Water-Use Efficiency

Water efficiency can be improved through:

  • Rainwater harvesting.
  • Farm ponds.
  • Soil-moisture conservation.
  • Drip and sprinkler irrigation.
  • Crop choice suited to local water availability.
📌 Must-Memorise

Water-Smart Agriculture → Right Crop + Right Water Use

41. Agricultural Productivity — Meaning

  • Agricultural productivity means output obtained per unit of input.
  • Land productivity is commonly measured as output per hectare.
📌 Must-Memorise

Land Productivity → Output per Hectare

42. Main Determinants of Productivity

Agricultural productivity depends on:

  • Soil quality.
  • Irrigation.
  • Seed quality.
  • Fertilisers.
  • Pest management.
  • Machinery.
  • Credit.
  • Extension.
  • Market access.

43. Improved Seeds and HYV

  • Improved seeds can increase yield and resistance to pests, disease and environmental stress.
  • HYV stands for High-Yielding Variety.
📌 Must-Memorise

HYV → High-Yielding Variety

44. NPK — Primary Fertiliser Nutrients

The three major fertiliser nutrients are:

  • Nitrogen.
  • Phosphorus.
  • Potassium.
📌 Must-Memorise

NPK → Nitrogen + Phosphorus + Potassium

45. Balanced Fertiliser Use

  • Balanced nutrient application supports soil health and crop productivity.
  • Excessive use of a single nutrient can reduce nutrient efficiency and damage soil quality.

46. Agricultural Mechanisation

Mechanisation includes:

  • Tractors.
  • Harvesters.
  • Pumps.
  • Seeders.
  • Threshers.
  • Other machinery.

Benefits include:

  • Timeliness.
  • Efficiency.
  • Precision.
  • Reduced peak-season labour shortages.

47. Mechanisation — Farm-Size Constraint

  • Machinery should be suited to farm size and local conditions.
  • Ownership of large machinery may be uneconomical for small and marginal farmers.

48. Custom Hiring

  • Custom hiring enables farmers to rent agricultural machinery instead of purchasing it.
  • It can improve access to mechanisation for small farmers.
📌 Must-Memorise

Custom Hiring → Rent Farm Machinery

49. Mechanisation — Employment Dimension

  • Mechanisation can reduce labour demand for some manual operations.
  • It should therefore be accompanied by skill development and expansion of rural non-farm employment.

50. Agricultural Extension

  • Agricultural extension transfers scientific knowledge and improved practices to farmers.

It can provide guidance on:

  • Crop choice.
  • Pest management.
  • Soil management.
  • Irrigation.
  • Mechanisation.
  • Market information.

51. Green Revolution — Meaning

  • The Green Revolution refers to the major increase in agricultural production achieved through modern agricultural technology.
  • It became especially important in India from the mid-1960s.
📌 Must-Memorise

Green Revolution in India → Mid-1960s Onward

52. Green Revolution — Technology Package

The Green Revolution combined:

  • HYV seeds.
  • Irrigation.
  • Chemical fertilisers.
  • Pesticides.
  • Agricultural credit.
  • Mechanisation.
  • Improved farm practices.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Green Revolution ≠ HYV Seeds Alone

53. Green Revolution — Wheat Advantage

  • Wheat benefited especially during the early phase of the Green Revolution.

54. M. S. Swaminathan

  • M. S. Swaminathan is closely associated with India's Green Revolution.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indian Green Revolution → M. S. Swaminathan

55. Norman Borlaug

  • Norman Borlaug is closely associated with high-yielding wheat varieties and the wider global Green Revolution.
📌 Must-Memorise

Global Green Revolution → Norman Borlaug

56. Green Revolution — Major Achievements

Important achievements included:

  • Increased food-grain production.
  • Greater food self-sufficiency.
  • Improved national food security.
  • Higher yields in irrigated regions.

57. Green Revolution — Major Limitations

Major concerns included:

  • Regional inequality.
  • Early concentration in wheat-growing regions.
  • Heavy fertiliser use.
  • Pesticide-related concerns.
  • Groundwater depletion.
  • Environmental stress.

58. Agricultural Credit — Why It Is Needed

Farmers require credit for:

  • Seeds.
  • Fertilisers.
  • Labour.
  • Machinery.
  • Irrigation.
  • Land development.
  • Livestock.
  • Equipment.

59. Formal and Informal Agricultural Credit

Formal sources include:

  • Commercial banks.
  • Cooperative banks.
  • Regional Rural Banks.
  • Other regulated institutions.

Informal sources include:

  • Moneylenders.
  • Traders.
  • Landlords.
  • Relatives.
  • Friends.

60. Agricultural Credit — Access Constraints

Formal credit may be restricted by:

  • Lack of collateral.
  • Weak land records.
  • Informal tenancy.
  • Low financial literacy.
  • Seasonal and irregular farm income.

61. NABARD

  • NABARD stands for National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development.
  • It is an important development financial institution supporting agriculture, rural credit and rural development.
📌 Must-Memorise

NABARD → National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

NABARD ≠ Ordinary Retail Commercial Bank

62. Kisan Credit Card — KCC

  • KCC stands for Kisan Credit Card.
  • It provides eligible farmers access to short-term and related agricultural credit through the formal banking system.
📌 Must-Memorise

KCC → Kisan Credit Card

63. Agricultural Marketing — Meaning

Agricultural marketing covers movement of produce from farm to final consumer or processor.

It includes:

  • Grading.
  • Storage.
  • Transport.
  • Processing.
  • Wholesale trade.
  • Retail trade.

64. APMC

  • APMC stands for Agricultural Produce Market Committee.
  • Agricultural marketing through APMCs is substantially governed by State laws.
📌 Must-Memorise

APMC → Agricultural Produce Market Committee

65. Farmer Price Problems

Farmers may receive lower prices because of:

  • Poor market information.
  • Lack of storage.
  • High transport costs.
  • Weak bargaining power.

66. Distress Sale

  • Distress sale occurs when a farmer is compelled to sell produce quickly at an unfavourable price.

67. Warehousing and Storage

  • Warehousing allows farmers to delay sale instead of selling immediately after harvest.
  • Better storage reduces post-harvest losses.

68. Grading and Standardisation

  • Grading classifies produce according to quality.
  • Standardisation improves transparency and can support better price realisation.

69. Electronic Agricultural Markets

Digital market platforms can improve:

  • Buyer-seller connectivity.
  • Price information.
  • Market access.

They work best when supported by:

  • Physical markets.
  • Logistics.
  • Grading.
  • Storage.
  • Reliable internet.

70. MSP — Minimum Support Price

  • MSP stands for Minimum Support Price.
  • It is a government-announced support price for specified crops intended to protect farmers against sharp market-price declines.
📌 Must-Memorise

MSP → Minimum Support Price

71. MSP vs Procurement

  • MSP → Announced support price.
  • Procurement → Actual purchase by government agencies.
📌 Must-Memorise

MSP ≠ Procurement

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

MSP ≠ Guaranteed Universal Purchase of Every Crop

72. Government Procurement

  • Procurement varies substantially across crops and regions.
  • It is particularly important for selected food grains.
  • Procurement supports buffer stocks and food-security operations.

73. CACP

  • CACP stands for Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices.
  • It advises the Union Government regarding MSPs.
📌 Must-Memorise

CACP → Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices

74. CACP — Factors Considered

CACP considers factors such as:

  • Production costs.
  • Demand and supply.
  • Price trends.
  • Inter-crop price relationships.

75. CACP vs Government

  • CACP advises on MSP.
  • The Government makes the final MSP announcement.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

CACP → Advises

Government → Announces

76. Agricultural Diversification — Meaning

  • Agricultural diversification means expanding rural production beyond a narrow range of crops.
  • It can reduce risk and improve income stability.

77. Major Diversification Activities

Important options include:

  • Horticulture.
  • Dairy.
  • Poultry.
  • Fisheries.
  • Sericulture.
  • Beekeeping.
  • Agroforestry.
  • Food processing.

78. Horticulture

Horticulture includes:

  • Fruits.
  • Vegetables.
  • Flowers.
  • Spices.
  • Plantation crops.
  • Many horticultural crops can generate high income per unit of land.
  • They often require better storage, transport and cold-chain infrastructure.

79. White Revolution

  • The White Revolution refers to rapid expansion of milk production.
  • It is closely associated with Operation Flood.
📌 Must-Memorise

White Revolution → Milk → Operation Flood

80. Verghese Kurien

  • Dr. Verghese Kurien is closely associated with the White Revolution and Operation Flood.
📌 Must-Memorise

White Revolution → Verghese Kurien

81. Dairy — Rural Income Role

  • Dairy can provide relatively regular income compared with highly seasonal crop farming.
  • It is an important component of rural livelihood diversification.

82. Blue Revolution

  • The Blue Revolution is associated with expansion and modernisation of fisheries and aquaculture.
📌 Must-Memorise

Blue Revolution → Fisheries + Aquaculture

83. Fisheries and Aquaculture

Marine fisheries, inland fisheries and aquaculture contribute to:

  • Food.
  • Employment.
  • Rural and coastal livelihoods.
  • Exports.

84. Food Security — Meaning

  • Food security means reliable physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food.

Its four main dimensions are:

  • Availability.
  • Access.
  • Utilisation.
  • Stability.
📌 Must-Memorise

Food Security → Availability + Access + Utilisation + Stability

85. Food Production vs Food Security

  • High food production alone does not guarantee food security.
  • Households must also possess access, purchasing power, nutrition and stability of supply.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Food Production ≠ Complete Food Security

86. FCI — Food Corporation of India

FCI plays an important role in:

  • Procurement.
  • Storage.
  • Movement.
  • Distribution of food grains.
📌 Must-Memorise

FCI → Food Corporation of India

87. Buffer Stocks

  • Buffer stocks are government-held food-grain reserves.
  • They support food security and supply management during shortages.

88. Public Distribution System — PDS

  • PDS stands for Public Distribution System.
  • It distributes specified commodities through fair-price shops under the applicable framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

PDS → Public Distribution System

89. Food-Management Chain

Production

→ Procurement

→ Storage

→ Buffer Stock

→ Distribution

📌 Must-Memorise

MSP → Procurement → FCI → Buffer Stocks → PDS

90. Soil Health

Healthy agricultural soil requires:

  • Adequate organic matter.
  • Balanced nutrients.
  • Suitable pH.
  • Biological activity.

91. Integrated Nutrient Management

  • Integrated nutrient management combines different nutrient sources to maintain soil fertility.

It can include:

  • Chemical fertilisers.
  • Organic manures.
  • Crop residues.
  • Biofertilisers.
  • Other nutrient sources.

92. Integrated Pest Management — IPM

  • IPM stands for Integrated Pest Management.
  • It combines biological, cultural, mechanical and selective chemical methods.
📌 Must-Memorise

IPM → Integrated Pest Management

93. Organic Farming

  • Organic farming restricts synthetic fertilisers and pesticides according to prescribed standards.
  • It relies more heavily on organic manures, crop rotations and biological processes.

94. Natural Farming

  • Natural farming seeks to minimise external chemical inputs and rely more strongly on locally available biological and ecological processes.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Organic Farming ≠ Automatically Same as Natural Farming

95. Climate-Resilient Agriculture

Climate-resilient agriculture can include:

  • Drought-tolerant crops.
  • Efficient irrigation.
  • Crop diversification.
  • Weather information.
  • Soil-moisture conservation.
  • Insurance.

96. Tamil Nadu — Major Agricultural Features

Tamil Nadu agriculture includes:

  • Paddy.
  • Sugarcane.
  • Groundnut.
  • Cotton.
  • Millets.
  • Pulses.
  • Banana.
  • Coconut.
  • Turmeric.
  • Horticulture.
  • Livestock.
  • Fisheries.

97. Tamil Nadu — Irrigation Sources

Tamil Nadu agriculture uses:

  • Rivers.
  • Reservoirs.
  • Tanks.
  • Wells.
  • Groundwater.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu → Strong Tank-Irrigation Tradition

98. Cauvery Delta

  • The Cauvery Delta is one of Tamil Nadu's major agricultural regions.
  • It is particularly associated with paddy cultivation.
  • Availability of Cauvery water strongly influences cultivation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cauvery Delta → Paddy

99. Tamil Nadu — Dryland Agriculture

Semi-arid parts of Tamil Nadu depend significantly on dryland farming.

Important dryland crops include:

  • Millets.
  • Pulses.
  • Oilseeds.
  • Other drought-suited crops.

100. Tamil Nadu — Horticulture and Plantation Crops

Important crops include:

  • Banana.
  • Mango.
  • Coconut.
  • Turmeric.
  • Tapioca.
  • Flowers.
  • Tea.
  • Coffee.

101. Tamil Nadu — Livestock, Poultry and Fisheries

Tamil Nadu has important:

  • Dairy activities.
  • Livestock economy.
  • Poultry production.
  • Marine fisheries.
  • Inland fisheries.
  • Aquaculture.

102. Major Agricultural Challenges

Important challenges include:

  • Small and fragmented holdings.
  • Rain-fed vulnerability.
  • Drought.
  • Groundwater depletion.
  • Water-intensive cropping.
  • Uneven productivity.
  • Price volatility.
  • Post-harvest losses.
  • Climate change.

103. Climate Change — Agricultural Effects

Climate change can affect agriculture through:

  • Higher temperatures.
  • Changed rainfall patterns.
  • Floods.
  • Droughts.
  • Water scarcity.
  • Crop-yield instability.

104. Agricultural Price Volatility

Farm prices can change because of:

  • Production.
  • Demand.
  • Imports.
  • Exports.
  • Weather.
  • Farmers may face sharp price falls immediately after harvest.

105. Post-Harvest Losses

Losses can be particularly serious for:

  • Fruits and vegetables.
  • Milk.
  • Fish.

Reducing losses requires:

  • Storage.
  • Cold chains.
  • Processing.
  • Reliable transport.

106. Farm Income — Main Determinants

Farm income depends on:

  • Yield.
  • Output prices.
  • Input costs.
  • Farm size.
  • Diversification.
  • Market access.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Higher Output ≠ Automatically Higher Farmer Income

121. TNPSC Traps

  • Agriculture belongs to the primary sector.
  • Declining GDP share does not make agriculture unimportant.
  • Kharif and Rabi are cropping seasons, not irrigation systems.
  • Kharif is associated with the southwest monsoon.
  • Rabi is the winter cropping season.
  • Zaid falls between Rabi and Kharif.
  • Rice is an important Kharif crop.
  • Wheat is primarily a Rabi crop.
  • Millets generally need less water than paddy.
  • Pulses provide plant protein.
  • Rhizobium is linked with nitrogen fixation in pulses.
  • Cotton is a fibre crop.
  • Cotton is associated with black soil in many regions.
  • Sugarcane requires substantial water.
  • Tea and coffee are plantation crops.
  • Coffee is concentrated mainly in southern India.
  • Irrigation reduces rainfall dependence.
  • Excessive groundwater use can deplete aquifers.
  • Tamil Nadu has an important tank-irrigation tradition.
  • Drip and sprinkler irrigation are different.
  • NPK means nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
  • Green Revolution was a package, not HYV seeds alone.
  • M. S. Swaminathan → Indian Green Revolution.
  • Norman Borlaug → Global Green Revolution.
  • Wheat benefited strongly during the early Green Revolution.
  • NABARD is a development financial institution.
  • KCC means Kisan Credit Card.

  • Agriculture belongs to which sector? → Primary sector.
  • Main roles of agriculture? → Food, employment, raw materials, rural income and livelihood security.
  • Does lower GDP share mean agriculture is unimportant? → No.
  • Three cropping seasons? → Kharif, Rabi and Zaid.
  • Kharif linked with? → Southwest monsoon.
  • Rabi linked with? → Winter.
  • Zaid occurs when? → Between Rabi and Kharif.
  • Important Kharif crop? → Rice.
  • Important Rabi crop? → Wheat.
  • Millets suited to? → Dry and semi-arid regions.
  • Millets use more or less water than paddy? → Generally less.
  • Pulses rich in? → Plant protein.
  • Pulses improve soil through? → Biological nitrogen fixation.
  • Bacteria linked with pulses? → Rhizobium.
  • Cotton type? → Fibre crop.
  • Cotton soil association? → Black soil.
  • Sugarcane used for? → Sugar, jaggery and ethanol.
  • Main oilseeds? → Groundnut, mustard, soybean, sunflower and sesame.
  • Tea-producing regions? → Assam, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Kerala.
  • Leading coffee-producing region in source? → Karnataka.
  • Irrigation means? → Artificial supply of water to crops.
  • Main irrigation sources? → Canals, wells, tube wells, tanks and reservoirs.
  • Groundwater overuse causes? → Aquifer depletion.
  • Tamil Nadu's important traditional irrigation system? → Tanks.
  • Drip irrigation supplies water where? → Near plant roots.
  • Sprinkler resembles? → Rainfall.
  • Agricultural productivity means? → Output per unit of input.
  • Land productivity? → Output per hectare.
  • NPK? → Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
  • HYV full form? → High-Yielding Variety.
  • Green Revolution in India? → Especially from mid-1960s.
  • Green Revolution package? → HYV + irrigation + fertilisers + pesticides + credit + mechanisation + better practices.
  • Crop strongly benefiting initially? → Wheat.
  • Indian Green Revolution personality? → M. S. Swaminathan.
  • Global Green Revolution personality? → Norman Borlaug.
  • NABARD full form? → National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development.
  • KCC full form? → Kisan Credit Card.
  • Formal agricultural credit sources? → Commercial banks, cooperative banks and RRBs.
  • APMC full form? → Agricultural Produce Market Committee.
  • MSP full form? → Minimum Support Price.
  • MSP and procurement same? → No.
  • Does MSP guarantee purchase of every crop from every farmer? → No.
  • CACP full form? → Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices.
  • Who advises on MSP? → CACP.
  • Who announces MSP? → Government.
  • White Revolution? → Milk.
  • Operation Flood? → White Revolution.
  • Verghese Kurien? → White Revolution.
  • Blue Revolution? → Fisheries and aquaculture.
  • Custom hiring? → Renting farm machinery.
  • Four food-security dimensions? → Availability, access, utilisation and stability.
  • FCI full form? → Food Corporation of India.
  • Buffer stock? → Government-held food-grain reserve.
  • PDS full form? → Public Distribution System.
  • IPM full form? → Integrated Pest Management.
  • Organic and natural farming same? → No.
  • Climate-resilient agriculture? → Farming adapted to climate and weather risks.
  • Important Tamil Nadu crops? → Paddy, sugarcane, groundnut, cotton, millets, pulses, banana, coconut and turmeric.
  • Major Tamil Nadu paddy region? → Cauvery Delta.
  • Tamil Nadu traditional irrigation? → Tanks.
  • Important allied Tamil Nadu activities? → Horticulture, livestock, poultry, marine fisheries, inland fisheries and aquaculture.
  • Core agriculture chain? → Land + Water + Seeds + Inputs + Credit + Technology + Labour + Markets.
